known_pitfalls.claim: A machine creates extra force or free energy.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter explains that machines redistribute force or speed. In real machines some input work is lost to friction, so efficiency is below 100%.

known_pitfalls.claim: Mechanical advantage of a wheel and axle is the axle radius divided by the wheel radius.
known_pitfalls.correction: For the arrangement used in this chapter, M.A. = radius of wheel / radius of axle. A larger wheel and smaller axle give greater ideal mechanical advantage.

known_pitfalls.claim: The steering example proves that only 120 N of work is needed instead of 1200 N of work.
known_pitfalls.correction: The example compares forces, not total work. In an ideal machine the smaller effort acts through a greater distance so that input and output work are equal.

known_pitfalls.claim: Tension always equals the weight of an attached object.
known_pitfalls.correction: Tension equals weight only when the hanging object has zero acceleration. For upward acceleration, T = m(g+a); for downward acceleration, T = m(g-a).

known_pitfalls.claim: In a two-mass pulley, each mass can have a different acceleration.
known_pitfalls.correction: For the ideal single string used in the chapter, both connected masses have the same acceleration magnitude because the string constrains their motion.

known_pitfalls.claim: Equal masses on the two sides of a pulley must move because gravity acts on both.
known_pitfalls.correction: Equal weights produce balanced forces, so the system remains at rest or continues at constant speed; there is no net driving force.

recommended_example_progression: Use Activity 4.1 to distinguish force multiplication from the creation of energy.
Use Activity 4.2 to explain why a large steering wheel and small axle increase torque and ideal mechanical advantage.
Use the steering-system Example to calculate M.A. = 10 and effort = 120 N.
Use the Quick Check gear-train data to combine two 60:1 ratios and convert the resulting hour-gear size to metres.
Use Activity 4.3 to compare string stretch for lighter and heavier bobs and identify the direction of tension.
Complete the 'Let us Calculate' pulley setup for 0.55 kg and 0.50 kg to find common acceleration and tension.
Use Examples 1 and 2 in Section 4.3 to compare stationary and upward-accelerating tension.
Use Check Your Understanding Q5 to solve the 2 kg and 6 kg frictionless-pulley system.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The supplied chapter ends with 'Check Your Understanding', questions 1-5, following the tension examples in Section 4.3.

beyond_the_textbook: Power steering systems add hydraulic or electric assistance, but the steering wheel and column still use the geometric advantage of applying force at a larger radius.
Bicycle gear systems let riders choose between greater wheel torque for climbing and greater wheel speed for travelling quickly on level roads.
Cranes often combine several pulleys so that the load is supported by multiple rope segments, reducing the effort force while increasing the rope distance pulled.
Engineers use bearings and lubrication to reduce friction, improving efficiency and limiting wear in wheels, axles, and pulleys.

Real ropes have mass and can stretch, while classroom pulley problems usually idealise the rope as massless and inextensible so that tension is uniform and connected objects share one acceleration magnitude.
